summary: Specifies extensions to HTTP authentication for interactive clients, so web applications need not build their own login systems with HTML forms. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: Normally every website builds its own login page. This tries to put a better login into the browser itself.

questions: replace html form login with http auth
how to add logout to http auth
subtitle: Extensions for HTTP authentication to support modern web applications.

tldr.problem: Modern web applications cannot use standard HTTP authentication (Basic or Digest) because it lacks features like optional login, logout, and flexible redirects. So they build custom authentication with HTML forms and cookies, sacrificing security.
tldr.mechanism: Two new HTTP headers extend authentication: Optional-WWW-Authenticate allows offering login without requiring it, and Authentication-Control provides parameters to control UI, redirects, timeouts, and suggested usernames.
tldr.outcome: Servers can now offer HTTP-level authentication competitive with form-based login, letting browsers handle authentication securely instead of relying on server-side JavaScript.

today: RFC 8053 is Experimental. While it has not been adopted as a standard, it provides extensions that modern browsers could support to improve web authentication. It remains the primary proposed solution for extending HTTP authentication to match form-based login features while preserving the security benefits of HTTP-level authentication.

sections.title: The Problem with Standard HTTP Authentication
sections.content:
HTTP has had built-in authentication for decades via Basic and Digest methods. But modern web applications need features that these schemes do not support:

Optional login (guests and registered users on the same page), logout from the browser side, redirects based on authentication status, and UI preferences (modal vs. non-modal dialogs). Because HTTP authentication is too rigid, nearly every website implements its own authentication using HTML form submission and cookies, with JavaScript validation on the server.

This custom approach has a critical weakness: the server controls all authentication logic. Cryptographically secure mechanisms and client-side defenses cannot be properly integrated. Form-based authentication is also vulnerable to phishing because the browser cannot visually distinguish between the site's login page and a fake one.

This RFC extends HTTP authentication to close the gap, allowing web applications to use HTTP-level authentication with the flexibility of form-based systems.
sections.eli5: When you visit a website, it usually shows you a custom login page with HTML text boxes. This is insecure because the server controls everything. The browser has built-in login features, but websites do not use them because the old HTTP login is too limited.

sections.title: Two New HTTP Headers
sections.content:
The RFC introduces two headers to extend authentication:

Optional-WWW-Authenticate is sent with 200 OK (not 401) when login is optional. It signals that the user may authenticate if they wish, but the page is usable without login. Old browsers that do not support this extension ignore the header and show the page normally. Compliant browsers prompt the user to log in.

Authentication-Control is sent by the server to provide fine-grained control over the authentication UI and behavior. It contains a list of parameters such as auth-style (modal or non-modal), location-when-unauthenticated (redirect URL if login is required), logout-timeout (seconds before the browser should forget credentials), and username (hint for login dialog).

These headers are backward compatible: old clients simply ignore them. New clients use them to provide a better user experience without JavaScript.
sections.eli5: The RFC defines two new instructions the server can send to the browser: one that says "login is optional here" and another that says "here is how you should show the login dialog."

sections.title: Authentication Parameters and Behavior
sections.content:
The Authentication-Control header can include several parameters:

auth-style tells the browser how to present the login dialog: modal (interrupt the page and ask for login first) or non-modal (show the page first, offer login as an option).

location-when-unauthenticated tells the browser to redirect unauthenticated users to a login page instead of prompting inline.

no-auth suppresses authentication attempts, useful for pages that want to display content before offering login.

location-when-logout specifies where the browser should go when the user clicks logout.

logout-timeout is the number of seconds before the browser automatically forgets login credentials (a security measure against console takeover).

username suggests a username to pre-fill in the login dialog (useful for network appliances with fixed admin usernames).

The state diagram in the RFC shows the complete flow: unauthenticated requests, authentication-initializing responses, intermediate responses (for schemes like Digest that require multiple round trips), and successfully authenticated or negatively authenticated responses.
sections.eli5: The server can tell the browser things like "show the login dialog as a popup" or "send the user to this page before asking for login" or "forget the password after 5 minutes."

sections.title: Deployment Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows three use cases:

Portal sites (like news sites) allow guest access but offer login to customize content. Optional authentication on all guest pages with auth-style=non-modal lets users read freely and opt in to login.

Authenticated-only sites (like banking) require login for all pages. Mandatory authentication with non-modal style and location-when-logout pointing to a goodbye page provides a clean flow.

Transition deployments can mix HTTP authentication with legacy form-based login. The server detects which method the client supports and provides fallbacks for old browsers.

The RFC emphasizes that all these parameters are hints, not security measures. Old or malicious clients can ignore them. Servers must still validate authentication on the server side and use cookies or other session mechanisms for long-term security.
sections.eli5: A news site can say "read for free, or log in for customized content." A bank site can say "you must log in to see your account." And a site can support both new HTTP login and old form login at the same time.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that these headers are not security measures. They provide user experience benefits and client-side convenience (like automatic logout after timeout), but servers cannot rely on them for protection.

The username parameter has special security concerns: sending valid usernames to unauthenticated users can aid attackers in guessing credentials. The RFC restricts its use to cases where the username is already public knowledge (like admin on a router whose manual is public) or where the username is unchangeable and the device is only accessible on a private network.

Servers MUST NOT use the logout timeout to enforce session limits on the server side. That must be done with cookies or session tokens. The timeout only helps prevent console takeover attacks.

All parameters SHOULD NOT be used for security enforcement. Clients can ignore them, so servers must always validate credentials and implement proper session management independently.
sections.eli5: These headers help the browser give users a better experience, but the server still has to enforce all the real security. A browser could ignore these instructions, so the server cannot trust them.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Extensions
sections.content:
The design prioritizes backward compatibility. Old HTTP clients simply ignore the new headers and see the page content. No existing functionality breaks.

The RFC allows extensions through two mechanisms: IANA-registered bare-tokens for standard parameters, and extension-tokens with the format -token.domain for private extensions. This allows vendors to experiment with new parameters without conflicting with others.

Interoperability with cookies is discussed: the RFC recommends using HTTP authentication for authorization decisions (who can access what) and cookies for session management (identifying multiple concurrent sessions for one user or tracking long-term state). This keeps concerns separated.
sections.eli5: Old websites keep working. New websites can use these headers. And vendors can add their own custom parameters with private names.
